claim: More than 70 genes have been linked to deafness.
source: While more than 70 genes have been linked to deafness, most of which are expressed in mechanosensory hair cells of the inner ear, a challenge has been to link these genes into molecular pathways.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, likely based on established scientific knowledge and literature.

claim: Most deafness genes are expressed in mechanosensory hair cells of the inner ear.
source: While more than 70 genes have been linked to deafness, most of which are expressed in mechanosensory hair cells of the inner ear, a challenge has been to link these genes into molecular pathways.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the expression patterns of deafness genes.

claim: Deafness mutations in Myo7a affect the development and function of stereocilia.
source: One example is Myo7a (myosin VIIA), in which deafness mutations affect the development and function of the mechanically sensitive stereocilia of hair cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research cited throughout the manuscript and represents established knowledge about Myo7a.

claim: MYO7A forms a complex with PDZD7.
source: Using this procedure, combined with identification and quantitation of proteins with mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that MYO7A forms a complex with PDZD7, a paralog of USH1C and DFNB31.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Figures 3-5.

claim: PDZD7 is a paralog of USH1C and DFNB31.
source: Using this procedure, combined with identification and quantitation of proteins with mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that MYO7A forms a complex with PDZD7, a paralog of USH1C and DFNB31.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary relationship between these proteins.

claim: MYO7A and PDZD7 interact in tissue-culture cells.
source: MYO7A and PDZD7 interact in tissue-culture cells, and co-localize to the ankle-link region of stereocilia in wild-type but not Myo7a mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and nanoscale pull-down experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: MYO7A and PDZD7 co-localize to the ankle-link region of stereocilia in wild-type mice.
source: MYO7A and PDZD7 interact in tissue-culture cells, and co-localize to the ankle-link region of stereocilia in wild-type but not Myo7a mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: MYO7A and PDZD7 do not co-localize to the ankle-link region in Myo7a mutant mice.
source: MYO7A and PDZD7 interact in tissue-culture cells, and co-localize to the ankle-link region of stereocilia in wild-type but not Myo7a mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data in Myo7a8J/8J mice shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Hair cells transduce mechanical signals evoked by sound and head movement.
source: Hair cells are the sensory cells of the inner ear; they transduce mechanical signals evoked by sound and head movement and relay these signals to the central nervous system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell function.

claim: Hair cells relay signals to the central nervous system.
source: Hair cells are the sensory cells of the inner ear; they transduce mechanical signals evoked by sound and head movement and relay these signals to the central nervous system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell function.

claim: The hair bundle is a cluster of approximately 100 actin-filled stereocilia.
source: The mechanically sensitive organelle responsible for mechanotransduction is the hair bundle, a cluster of ~100 actin-filled stereocilia that protrude apically from a hair cell (Gillespie and Müller, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gillespie and Müller, 2009.

claim: Stereocilia protrude apically from a hair cell.
source: The mechanically sensitive organelle responsible for mechanotransduction is the hair bundle, a cluster of ~100 actin-filled stereocilia that protrude apically from a hair cell (Gillespie and Müller, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gillespie and Müller, 2009.

claim: Stereocilia bend at their bases.
source: Because stereocilia bend at their bases yet are coupled together with elastic linkages, the bundle pivots as a whole when exposed to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stereocilia mechanics.

claim: Stereocilia are coupled together with elastic linkages.
source: Because stereocilia bend at their bases yet are coupled together with elastic linkages, the bundle pivots as a whole when exposed to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stereocilia structure.

claim: The hair bundle pivots as a whole when exposed to mechanical stimuli.
source: Because stereocilia bend at their bases yet are coupled together with elastic linkages, the bundle pivots as a whole when exposed to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair bundle mechanics.

claim: The tip link is composed of a dimer of CDH23 molecules interacting with a dimer of PCDH15 molecules.
source: The tip link is composed of a dimer of CDH23 (cadherin 23) molecules interacting with a dimer of PCDH15 (protocadherin 15) molecules (Kazmierczak et al., 2007), and is coupled to the mechanically sensitive transduction channel.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kazmierczak et al., 2007.

claim: The tip link is coupled to the mechanically sensitive transduction channel.
source: The tip link is composed of a dimer of CDH23 (cadherin 23) molecules interacting with a dimer of PCDH15 (protocadherin 15) molecules (Kazmierczak et al., 2007), and is coupled to the mechanically sensitive transduction channel.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kazmierczak et al., 2007.

claim: Ankle links couple stereocilia together at their bases.
source: Another class of linkage, the ankle link, couples stereocilia together at their bases, transiently in auditory hair cells but persistently in vestibular hair cells (Goodyear and Richardson, 1999; Adato et al., 2005; McGee et al., 2006; Michalski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ankle links are transient in auditory hair cells.
source: Another class of linkage, the ankle link, couples stereocilia together at their bases, transiently in auditory hair cells but persistently in vestibular hair cells (Goodyear and Richardson, 1999; Adato et al., 2005; McGee et al., 2006; Michalski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ankle links are persistent in vestibular hair cells.
source: Another class of linkage, the ankle link, couples stereocilia together at their bases, transiently in auditory hair cells but persistently in vestibular hair cells (Goodyear and Richardson, 1999; Adato et al., 2005; McGee et al., 2006; Michalski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: MYO7A was the first protein involved in hair-cell mechanotransduction to be identified by genetics.
source: Myosin VIIA (MYO7A) was the first protein involved in hair-cell mechanotransduction to be identified by genetics (Gibson et al., 1995; Weil et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gibson et al., 1995 and Weil et al., 1996.

claim: MYO7A has been implicated in ankle-link positioning by its location in frog stereocilia.
source: While MYO7A has been implicated in ankle-link positioning by its location in frog stereocilia (Hasson et al., 1997) and by mislocalization of ankle-link proteins in Myo7a-null mice (Michalski et al., 2007), more precise localization experiments suggested that MYO7A also participates in mechanotransduction (Grati and Kachar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hasson et al., 1997.

claim: Ankle-link proteins are mislocalized in Myo7a-null mice.
source: While MYO7A has been implicated in ankle-link positioning by its location in frog stereocilia (Hasson et al., 1997) and by mislocalization of ankle-link proteins in Myo7a-null mice (Michalski et al., 2007), more precise localization experiments suggested that MYO7A also participates in mechanotransduction (Grati and Kachar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Michalski et al., 2007.

claim: MYO7A participates in mechanotransduction.
source: While MYO7A has been implicated in ankle-link positioning by its location in frog stereocilia (Hasson et al., 1997) and by mislocalization of ankle-link proteins in Myo7a-null mice (Michalski et al., 2007), more precise localization experiments suggested that MYO7A also participates in mechanotransduction (Grati and Kachar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grati and Kachar, 2011.

claim: MYO7A could form several different protein complexes to reconcile its differing roles.
source: These differing roles could be reconciled if MYO7A forms several different protein complexes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on inference from the data.

claim: The tail of MYO7A has two tandem FERM-MyTH4 domains and one SH3 domain.
source: The tail of MYO7A has two tandem FERM-MyTH4 domains and one SH3 domain, each of which might interact with stereocilia proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MYO7A structure.

claim: Each domain of MYO7A tail might interact with stereocilia proteins.
source: The tail of MYO7A has two tandem FERM-MyTH4 domains and one SH3 domain, each of which might interact with stereocilia proteins.
evidence: This is speculation about potential interactions.

claim: MYO7A interacts with PCDH15.
source: Biochemical and structural studies have indicated that MYO7A interacts both with PCDH15 (Senften et al., 2006) and with a complex including USH1C, USH1G, and CDH23 (Boëda et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Senften et al., 2006.

claim: MYO7A interacts with a complex including USH1C, USH1G, and CDH23.
source: Biochemical and structural studies have indicated that MYO7A interacts both with PCDH15 (Senften et al., 2006) and with a complex including USH1C, USH1G, and CDH23 (Boëda et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boëda et al., 2002 and Wu et al., 2011.

claim: Preliminary evidence suggests that MYO7A interacts with ADGRV1.
source: Preliminary evidence suggests that MYO7A interacts with ADGRV1, which was formerly known as GPR98 and VLGR1 (Hamann et al., 2015), USH2A (usherin), and DFNB31 (whirlin) (Delprat et al., 2005; Michalski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hamann et al., 2015, Delprat et al., 2005, and Michalski et al., 2007.

claim: Preliminary evidence suggests that MYO7A interacts with USH2A.
source: Preliminary evidence suggests that MYO7A interacts with ADGRV1, which was formerly known as GPR98 and VLGR1 (Hamann et al., 2015), USH2A (usherin), and DFNB31 (whirlin) (Delprat et al., 2005; Michalski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Delprat et al., 2005 and Michalski et al., 2007.

claim: Preliminary evidence suggests that MYO7A interacts with DFNB31.
source: Preliminary evidence suggests that MYO7A interacts with ADGRV1, which was formerly known as GPR98 and VLGR1 (Hamann et al., 2015), USH2A (usherin), and DFNB31 (whirlin) (Delprat et al., 2005; Michalski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Delprat et al., 2005 and Michalski et al., 2007.

claim: No interactions of MYO7A have been reported with PDZD7.
source: No interactions of MYO7A have been reported with PDZD7, another member of the ankle-link complex (Grati et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014), and how MYO7A positions the ankle-link complex remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior reports in the literature.

claim: PDZD7 is a member of the ankle-link complex.
source: No interactions of MYO7A have been reported with PDZD7, another member of the ankle-link complex (Grati et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014), and how MYO7A positions the ankle-link complex remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grati et al., 2012 and Zou et al., 2014.

claim: How MYO7A positions the ankle-link complex remains unclear.
source: No interactions of MYO7A have been reported with PDZD7, another member of the ankle-link complex (Grati et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014), and how MYO7A positions the ankle-link complex remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Genetic methods can miss proteins that are more widely expressed or that can be compensated for by a paralog.
source: While genetic methods have been successful in identifying essential stereocilia proteins, the approach can miss proteins that are more widely expressed or that can be compensated for by the expression of a paralog.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of genetic approaches.

claim: The twist-off method is limited in throughput.
source: Because of the fine dissection and tissue manipulation required, however, the twist-off method is limited in its throughput and is less ideal for biochemical experiments examining rare protein-protein complexes in bundles.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of the twist-off method.

claim: The twist-off method is less ideal for biochemical experiments examining rare protein-protein complexes.
source: Because of the fine dissection and tissue manipulation required, however, the twist-off method is limited in its throughput and is less ideal for biochemical experiments examining rare protein-protein complexes in bundles.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of the twist-off method.

claim: The D10 antibody recognizes PTPRQ.
source: D10 recognizes PTPRQ (Goodyear et al., 2003), the most abundant transmembrane protein of hair bundles (Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goodyear et al., 2003.

claim: PTPRQ is the most abundant transmembrane protein of hair bundles.
source: D10 recognizes PTPRQ (Goodyear et al., 2003), the most abundant transmembrane protein of hair bundles (Shin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2013.

claim: DTSSP is a membrane-impermeable, reversible crosslinker.
source: In most cases, we treated the exposed surfaces of dissected inner ears with DTSSP, a membrane-impermeable, reversible crosslinker with two N-hydroxysuccinimide groups coupled with an 12 Å spacer that includes a disulfide bond (Staros, 1982, 1988); this treatment stabilizes complexes of membrane proteins (Corgiat et al., 2014), presumably including ankle links and tip links.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Staros, 1982, 1988.

claim: DTSSP treatment stabilizes complexes of membrane proteins.
source: In most cases, we treated the exposed surfaces of dissected inner ears with DTSSP, a membrane-impermeable, reversible crosslinker with two N-hydroxysuccinimide groups coupled with an 12 Å spacer that includes a disulfide bond (Staros, 1982, 1988); this treatment stabilizes complexes of membrane proteins (Corgiat et al., 2014), presumably including ankle links and tip links.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corgiat et al., 2014.

claim: DTSSP treatment should not affect intracellular protein complexes.
source: DTSSP treatment should not affect intracellular protein complexes, however, and is reversed by reduction.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of DTSSP as a membrane-impermeable crosslinker.

claim: DTSSP crosslinking is reversed by reduction.
source: DTSSP treatment should not affect intracellular protein complexes, however, and is reversed by reduction.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of DTSSP.

claim: Cytoplasmic proteins in association with membrane proteins can be detected if their binding affinity is sufficiently high.
source: If their binding affinity is sufficiently high, cytoplasmic proteins in association with membrane proteins should still be detected, however, even without covalent crosslinking.
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical principles.

claim: The D10 preparation enriches stereocilia membranes from chicks.
source: We enriched stereocilia membranes from chicks using the D10 preparation, named for the monoclonal antibody that is critical for the procedure (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: ATP2B2 is the plasma-membrane Ca2+ pump of stereocilia.
source: We used antibodies to ATP2B2, the plasma-membrane Ca2+ pump of stereocilia (Dumont et al., 2001), to locate fractions containing stereocilia membranes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dumont et al., 2001.

claim: Most of the ATP2B2 was detected in the RIPA-solubilized fraction S7.
source: Nearly all of the ATP2B2 was detected in S7, however, showing that stereocilia membranes were efficiently solubilized.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The total amount of actin and ATP2B2 per ear in the D10 preparation was much higher than in the twist-off preparation.
source: In quantitative immunoblotting experiments, we found that the total amount of actin and ATP2B2 per ear, as compared to the amount in a single utricle, was much higher in the D10 stereocilia membrane preparation than in the twist-off hair-bundle preparation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The elevated level of stereocilia protein in the D10 preparation derived in part from sampling seven organs.
source: This elevated level of stereocilia protein derived in part from sampling seven organs (cochlea, lagena, utricle, saccule, and three semicircular canals) rather than just one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: Contaminating ATP1A1 from the basolateral membrane was detectable in the D10 preparation at modest levels.
source: Contaminating ATP1A1 from the basolateral membrane was detectable in the D10 preparation, but at modest levels compared to that in one utricle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A major advantage of the D10 preparation is its high throughput.
source: The D10 and twist-off preparations were compared in Table 1; note that a major advantage of the D10 preparation is its high throughput.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Table 1.

claim: The total amount of protein decreased from approximately 110 mg in S1 to approximately 1 mg in S7.
source: In fractions from two independent preparations, each of 1000 chick ears, the total amount of protein (Table 2) decreased from ~110 mg in S1 (post-nuclear supernatant) to ~1 mg in S7 (RIPA solubilized membranes), consistent with the silver-stain analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the protein assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: Over 3000 proteins were detected in each fraction by shotgun mass spectrometry.
source: We analyzed two technical replicates each of the two preparations by shotgun mass spectrometry (four runs per fraction), and used Andromeda peptide searching and MaxQuant protein assembly and quantitation to determine the protein composition of each fraction. Equal amounts of protein were analyzed, and over 3000 proteins were detected in each fraction.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: PTPRQ had the largest enrichment slope in the D10 preparation.
source: Of the 3036 proteins detected in at least four of the six fractions, PTPRQ had the largest 'enrichment slope' (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the shotgun mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ten most enriched GO terms in S7 relative to S1 referred to membranes, mitochondria, or plasma membrane.
source: Gene ontology analysis (Ashburner et al., 2000; Gene Ontology Consortium, 2015) using DAVID (Huang et al., 2009b, 2009a) indicated that the ten most enriched GO terms in S7 relative to S1 referred to membranes, mitochondria, or plasma membrane (Figure 2B); the latter term was most highly enriched in the last enrichment fraction (p=3 × 10–6).
evidence: This is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The steeper the enrichment slope, the more likely a protein was annotated as containing a transmembrane helix.
source: In addition, the steeper the enrichment slope, the more likely a protein was annotated as containing a transmembrane helix (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The D10 preparation substantially enriches membranes, especially stereocilia membranes.
source: Taken together, our analysis shows that the D10 preparation substantially enriches membranes, especially stereocilia membranes, reducing protein complexity so that additional affinity purification steps can be used to identify protein complexes of stereocilia membranes.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry and gene ontology analyses.

claim: Stereocilia membranes account for approximately 5% of the solubilized membrane material in S7.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that stereocilia membranes account for ~5% of the solubilized membrane material in S7.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative abundance of marker proteins.

claim: Cluster 8 had the greatest enrichment slope and contained PTPRQ, ATP2B2, and XIRP2.
source: Cluster 8 had the greatest enrichment slope, and not surprisingly, it contained both PTPRQ and ATP2B2, as well as XIRP2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PTPRQ was enriched between S1 and S7 by around 50-fold using targeted proteomics.
source: Using this approach, we determined that PTPRQ was enriched between S1 and S7 by around 50-fold (Figure 2); the enrichment of ATP2B2 was less, perhaps because substantial amounts were located in hair-cell somas.
evidence: This is supported by the targeted proteomics data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: MYO7A is present in hair cell somas.
source: While MYO7A is also present in hair cell somas, a rough estimate based on the amount in chick hair bundles (Table 3) indicates that purification would require an enrichment of approximately 106-fold from dissected inner ears.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MYO7A localization.

claim: Purification of MYO7A from dissected inner ears would require an enrichment of approximately 10^6-fold.
source: While MYO7A is also present in hair cell somas, a rough estimate based on the amount in chick hair bundles (Table 3) indicates that purification would require an enrichment of approximately 106-fold from dissected inner ears.
evidence: This is an inference based on the abundance data in Table 3.

claim: The stereocilia-membrane enrichment provides approximately 10^2-fold purification.
source: The 102-fold purification afforded by the stereocilia-membrane enrichment indicates that additional affinity purification steps are required to bring MYO7A complex abundance to the level where it can be definitively detected in shotgun mass-spectrometry experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment data.

claim: The majority of MYO7A was in the insoluble fraction (P7) of the RIPA extraction.
source: We therefore used immunoaffinity methods to further enrich MYO7A after purification of stereocilia membranes (Figure 3A); although the majority of MYO7A was in the insoluble fraction (P7) of the RIPA extraction of D10 membranes, a substantial amount was solubilized (S7).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A substantial amount of MYO7A was solubilized in the S7 fraction.
source: We therefore used immunoaffinity methods to further enrich MYO7A after purification of stereocilia membranes (Figure 3A); although the majority of MYO7A was in the insoluble fraction (P7) of the RIPA extraction of D10 membranes, a substantial amount was solubilized (S7).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 138-1 monoclonal antibody recognizes chicken MYO7A.
source: For the subsequent step, we used the 138-1 monoclonal antibody, which recognizes chicken MYO7A (Soni et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soni et al., 2005.

claim: A MYO7A complex in stereocilia with USH1C, USH1G, and CDH23 is plausible.
source: Our combined immunoblotting and targeted proteomics data thus indicates that a MYO7A complex in stereocilia with USH1C, USH1G, and—probably—CDH23 is plausible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunoblotting and targeted proteomics data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PDZD7 was present at significantly greater levels in 138-1 precipitations than in control precipitations.
source: PDZD7 was present at significantly greater levels in 138-1 precipitations than in control precipitations (Figure 4H), confirming its specific precipitation with MYO7A.
evidence: This is supported by the targeted proteomics data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Only one peptide for ADGRV1 showed significant enrichment in 138-1 immunoprecipitates compared to controls.
source: By contrast, only one peptide for ADGRV1 showed significant enrichment in 138-1 immunoprecipitates compared to controls, and the fraction precipitated was very small (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by the targeted proteomics data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: PDZD7:MYO7A complexes are more abundant than ones containing ADGRV1, or ADGRV1 binds less tightly than PDZD7.
source: We suggest that PDZD7:MYO7A complexes are more abundant than ones containing ADGRV1, or that ADGRV1 binds less tightly than PDZD7.
evidence: This is speculation based on the targeted proteomics data.

claim: PDZD7 fused to mCherry was specifically immunoprecipitated by 138-1 along with GFP-MYO7A in HEK293 cells.
source: When detected using an anti-PDZD7 antibody, PDZD7 fused to mCherry was specifically immunoprecipitated by 138-1 along with GFP-MYO7A (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The MYO7A-PDZD7 stoichiometry was high, as the majority of the PDZD7 was immunoprecipitated.
source: The MYO7A-PDZD7 stoichiometry was high, as the majority of the PDZD7 was immunoprecipitated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ANKRD24 specifically co-immunoprecipitated with MYO7A.
source: ANKRD24 also specifically co-immunoprecipitated with MYO7A (Figure 5B), although a much lower fraction of the total ANKRD24 was recovered.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PDZD7 tagged with Strep-tag II did not co-immunoprecipitate with ANKRD24-GFP.
source: By contrast, PDZD7 tagged with Strep-tag II did not co-immunoprecipitate with ANKRD24-GFP, supporting the specificity of the interactions of PDZD7 and ANKRD24 with MYO7A (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No other proteins were co-precipitated at similar abundance to PDZD7 in HEK cells expressing MYO7A and PDZD7.
source: No other proteins were co-precipitated at similar abundance, with the exception of one abundant peptide for the protein FER1L1, which was also artifactually precipitated by 138-1 in the untransfected controls.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Co-expression of the MYO10HMM-MYO7Atail fusion with mCherry-USH1G led to robust targeting to filopodia tips.
source: Co-expression of the MYO10HMM-MYO7Atail fusion with mCherry-USH1G led to robust targeting to filopodia tips (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: mCherry-USH1C formed intracellular actin cables.
source: As seen previously, mCherry-USH1C formed intracellular actin cables; co-expressed MYO10HMM-MYO7Atail targeted there too (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: mCherry-PDZD7 targeted to filopodia tips only if MYO10HMM-MYO7Atail was expressed.
source: mCherry-PDZD7 targeted to filopodia tips, but only if MYO10HMM-MYO7Atail was expressed (Figure 6D); with a few exceptions, no mCherry-PDZD7 was clustered with the control construct MYO10HMM (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Only minimal amounts of ANKRD24-Strep targeted to filopodia.
source: By contrast, only minimal amounts of ANKRD24-Strep targeted to filopodia, confirming its interaction with the MYO7A tail was weak, nonexistent, or masked in tissue-culture cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Vestibular stereocilia of Myo7a8J/8J homozygotes were not arranged in a coherent bundle.
source: As previously reported, vestibular stereocilia of 8J/8J homozygotes were not arranged in a coherent bundle but instead projected randomly; moreover, stereocilia heights in Myo7a8J mice were irregular, with many stereocilia being longer than the longest stereocilia in wild-type mice (Figure 7B,F,M).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7B,F,M.

claim: Stereocilia heights in Myo7a8J mice were irregular.
source: As previously reported, vestibular stereocilia of 8J/8J homozygotes were not arranged in a coherent bundle but instead projected randomly; moreover, stereocilia heights in Myo7a8J mice were irregular, with many stereocilia being longer than the longest stereocilia in wild-type mice (Figure 7B,F,M).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7B,F,M.

claim: Stereocilia in Myo7a8J/8J mice were often arranged radially around the fonticulus.
source: Not only were stereocilia not arranged in a staircase manner, but unlike in wild-type bundles (Figure 7E), they were often arranged radially around the cytoplasmic channel where the kinocilium inserts, the fonticulus (Figure 7G, asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7E,G.

claim: The fonticulus was usually found in the center of cuticular plate in Myo7a8J/8J mice, indicating a loss of subcellular planar polarity.
source: The fonticulus was usually found in the center of cuticular plate, indicating a loss of subcellular planar polarity (Deans, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging data and supported by a citation to Deans, 2013.

claim: MYO7A localization in mouse vestibular hair bundles is punctate and often stronger near stereocilia tips.
source: To localize MYO7A, we used an antibody that did not label 8J/8J homozygous bundles (Figure 7B); this antibody produced punctate labeling that was often stronger near stereocilia tips (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: MYO7A bound along the periphery of the actin core, juxtaposed with the membrane.
source: To allow imaging of utricle stereocilia by superresolution microscopy with structured-illumination (Gustafsson, 2000), we isolated stereocilia by absorption to poly-L-lysine-coated coverslips (Neugebauer and Thurm, 1984, Hasson et al., 1997); these experiments showed that MYO7A bound along the periphery of the actin core, juxtaposed with the membrane (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by the structured-illumination microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The localization of ADGRV1 to the ankle link region in utricle hair bundles depended on functional MYO7A.
source: As previously reported for cochlea (Michalski et al., 2007), the localization of ADVGRV1 to the ankle link region in utricle hair bundles depended on functional MYO7A (Figure 7H–I).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7H-I and a citation to Michalski et al., 2007.

claim: Localization of ATP2B2 was unaffected in Myo7a8J/8J homozygous utricle bundles.
source: By contrast, localization of ATP2B2 was unaffected in 8J/8J homozygous utricle bundles (Figure 7J–K).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7J-K.

claim: MYO7A was punctate in cochlear hair cells, with weak labeling in hair bundle and stronger labeling in the cell soma.
source: MYO7A was punctate, with weak labeling in hair bundle, and stronger labeling in the cell soma (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is supported by the structured-illumination microscopy data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: Stereocilia of Myo7a8J/8J homozygotes were highly disorganized and had irregular lengths.
source: As previously reported (Self et al., 1998), stereocilia of 8J/8J homozygotes were highly disorganized and had irregular lengths; no MYO7A immunoreactivity was detected (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7M and a citation to Self et al., 1998.

claim: ATP2B2 localization in inner and outer hair cells was relatively normal in Myo7a8J/8J mice, despite the bundle disarray.
source: By contrast, ATP2B2 localization in inner and outer hair cells was relatively normal, despite the bundle disarray; in both heterozygotes and homozygotes, labeling was much stronger in outer hair cells than in inner hair cells (Dumont et al., 2001; Beurg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7N-O and citations to Dumont et al., 2001 and Beurg et al., 2010.

claim: PDZD7 localized to ankle links of heterozygous P8 Myo7a+/8J utricle hair cells.
source: As previously shown (Grati et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014), PDZD7 localized to ankle links of heterozygous P8 Myo7a+/8J utricle hair cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8A and citations to Grati et al., 2012 and Zou et al., 2014.

claim: Some cell bodies of hair cells had large amounts of PDZD7 immunoreactivity.
source: Some cell bodies of hair cells had large amounts of PDZD7 immunoreactivity (Figure 8A,F), and PDZD7 was located in the pericuticular necklace region and the funiculus (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8A,B,F.

claim: PDZD7 was located in the pericuticular necklace region and the funiculus.
source: Some cell bodies of hair cells had large amounts of PDZD7 immunoreactivity (Figure 8A,F), and PDZD7 was located in the pericuticular necklace region and the funiculus (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The pericuticular necklace region and funiculus have been implicated in vesicular trafficking.
source: Both regions have been implicated in vesicular trafficking.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these cellular regions.

claim: PDZD7 and MYO7A punctae occasionally overlap in utricle stereocilia.
source: Note that MYO7A and PDZD7 punctae occasionally overlap (yellow).
evidence: This is supported by the structured-illumination microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: mCherry-PDZD7 is located in the ankle-link region after in utero electroporation.
source: In two transfected utricles, we identified >20 transfected hair cells; the mCherry signal was low in all, but in cells with the highest expression of mCherry-PDZD7, the signal was clearly discernable at the base of the hair bundle (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Cells with the highest levels of mCherry-PDZD7 had very disorganized hair bundles after injectoporation.
source: Many cells were transfected, with a wide range of expression levels. Cells with the highest levels of mCherry signal had very disorganized hair bundles (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), a phenotype we rarely see in cells injectoporated with control plasmids (Xiong et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells with the lowest levels of mCherry-PDZD7 had mCherry-PDZD7 located specifically in hair bundles, largely at stereocilia bases.
source: By contrast, cells with the lowest levels of signal had mCherry-PDZD7 located specifically in hair bundles, largely at stereocilia bases (Figure 8H–I).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8H-I.

claim: PDZD7 depended on MYO7A for localization to ankle links.
source: PDZD7 depended on MYO7A for localization to ankle links (Figure 8J–O).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8J-O.

claim: PDZD7 was absent from the ankle-link region in Myo7a8J/8J homozygous utricles at P8.
source: While localization was normal in heterozygous Myo7a+/8J utricles (Figure 8J–K), when we examined 8J/8J homozygous Myo7a8J/8J utricles at P8, we noted that PDZD7 was absent from the ankle-link region, although it remained present in the apical region of hair cell somas (Figure 8L–M).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8L-M.

claim: PDZD7 labeling was prominent in the ankle-link region of bundles of heterozygous cochlear inner hair cells.
source: In the cochlea, PDZD7 labeling was prominent in the ankle-link region of bundles of heterozygous cochlear inner hair cells visualized using structured-illumination microscopy (Figure 8N).
evidence: This is supported by the structured-illumination microscopy data shown in Figure 8N.

claim: PDZD7 labeling was absent from homozygous Myo7a8J/8J cochlear bundles.
source: By contrast, PDZD7 labeling was absent from homozygous Myo7a8J/8J bundles (Figure 8O).
evidence: This is supported by the structured-illumination microscopy data shown in Figure 8O.

claim: MYO7A interacts with several scaffolding proteins.
source: Our results show that MYO7A interacts with several scaffolding proteins, which suggests that different MYO7A complexes may simultaneously mediate several functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry and immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Different MYO7A complexes may simultaneously mediate several functions.
source: Our results show that MYO7A interacts with several scaffolding proteins, which suggests that different MYO7A complexes may simultaneously mediate several functions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data showing multiple MYO7A interactions.

claim: PDZD7 is essential for the formation of the ankle-link protein complex.
source: We have focused here on PDZD7, which is essential for the formation of the ankle-link protein complex (Ebermann et al., 2010; Grati et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014) and requires MYO7A for localization to ankle links.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ebermann et al., 2010; Grati et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014.

claim: PDZD7 requires MYO7A for localization to ankle links.
source: We have focused here on PDZD7, which is essential for the formation of the ankle-link protein complex (Ebermann et al., 2010; Grati et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014) and requires MYO7A for localization to ankle links.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8.

claim: MYO7A is present in inner ear tissue in complexes with USH1C, USH1G, and CDH23.
source: We also showed that MYO7A is present in inner ear tissue in the predicted complexes with USH1C, USH1G, and CDH23.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The D10 preparation has significant contamination.
source: The D10 preparation has significant contamination, however; we estimate that stereocilia membranes account for only ~5% of the RIPA-solubilized material.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Contaminating intracellular organelles are disrupted by a freeze-thaw cycle.
source: Other membranes are present in part because contaminating intracellular organelles are disrupted by a freeze-thaw cycle, preventing their precise separation from stereocilia based on distinct, uniform sedimentation properties (Cox and Emili, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental procedure and supported by a citation to Cox and Emili, 2006.

claim: The D10 preparation maximizes total recovery of stereocilia membrane protein rather than purity.
source: Many of the most important stereocilia proteins are present at vanishingly small levels, however, so for stereocilia membrane enrichment, we chose to maximize total recovery of stereocilia membrane protein rather than purity.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: Immunoaffinity purification allows tremendous enrichment, even if multiple affinity enrichment steps are needed.
source: Immunoaffinity purification, especially with high-affinity monoclonal antibodies, allows tremendous enrichment, even if multiple affinity enrichment steps are ultimately needed for some stereocilia protein complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about immunoaffinity purification methods.

claim: DTSSP should enhance the ability to detect low-abundance membrane protein interactions.
source: We stabilized protein complexes of the stereocilia using chemical crosslinking with membrane-impermeant crosslinker DTSSP, which should enhance our ability to detect low-abundance membrane protein interactions (Vasilescu et al., 2004; Gokhale et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Corgiat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vasilescu et al., 2004; Gokhale et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012; Corgiat et al., 2014.

claim: Not all proteins precipitated with the 138-1 antibody are in specific complexes with MYO7A.
source: Were all proteins precipitated in our experiments with the 138-1 antibody in specific complexes with MYO7A? Probably not.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the method.

claim: Subsequent validation of interactions detected is of high importance.
source: Subsequent validation of interactions detected, for example showing co-immunoprecipitation, protein-protein binding, or mislocalization in mutant hair cells, is thus of high importance.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of validation experiments.

claim: PDZD7 has been identified as a nonsyndromic deafness gene.
source: Originally identified as a modifier gene for Usher syndrome type 2 genes, PDZD7 has more recently been identified as a nonsyndromic deafness gene itself (Booth et al., 2015; Vona et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Booth et al., 2015 and Vona et al., 2016.

claim: Positioning of ADGRV1 at ankle links depends critically on PDZD7.
source: Genetics experiments showed that positioning of ADGRV1 at ankle links depends critically on PDZD7 (Zou et al., 2014); consistent with those results, PDZD7 binds directly to ADGRV1 (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zou et al., 2014 and Chen et al., 2014.

claim: PDZD7 binds directly to ADGRV1.
source: Genetics experiments showed that positioning of ADGRV1 at ankle links depends critically on PDZD7 (Zou et al., 2014); consistent with those results, PDZD7 binds directly to ADGRV1 (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: PDZD7 could bind to MYO7A, and then MYO7A could transport the PDZD7-ADGRV1 complex to its final location.
source: Our experiments suggest how this positioning might occur; PDZD7 could bind to MYO7A, and then MYO7A could transport the PDZD7-ADGRV1 complex to its final location.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of PDZD7 and ADGRV1 localization.

claim: MYO7A is required for localization of ADGRV1.
source: MYO7A is also required for localization of ADGRV1; while MYO7A might bind directly to ADGRV1, the necessity of PDZD7 for the formation of the ankle-link complex suggests that MYO7A localizes both PDZD7 and ADGRV1 at ankle links.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and prior literature.

claim: MYO7A localizes both PDZD7 and ADGRV1 at ankle links.
source: MYO7A is also required for localization of ADGRV1; while MYO7A might bind directly to ADGRV1, the necessity of PDZD7 for the formation of the ankle-link complex suggests that MYO7A localizes both PDZD7 and ADGRV1 at ankle links.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and prior literature.

claim: MYO7A concentrates at the ankle-link region of vestibular stereocilia of mature frogs.
source: Association of MYO7A with ankle-link proteins explains the early observation that MYO7A concentrates at the ankle-link region of vestibular stereocilia of mature frogs (Hasson et al., 1997) and cochlea stereocilia of immature mice (Senften et al., 2006; Lëfevre et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hasson et al., 1997.

claim: MYO7A concentrates at the ankle-link region of cochlea stereocilia of immature mice.
source: Association of MYO7A with ankle-link proteins explains the early observation that MYO7A concentrates at the ankle-link region of vestibular stereocilia of mature frogs (Hasson et al., 1997) and cochlea stereocilia of immature mice (Senften et al., 2006; Lëfevre et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Senften et al., 2006 and Lëfevre et al., 2008.

claim: Positioning at the ankle-link location by MYO7A is surprising because the ankle links are very close to the pointed ends of the filaments.
source: Positioning at this location by MYO7A is surprising, however, as the ankle links are very close to the pointed ends of the filaments located at the periphery of the stereocilia actin core.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structure of stereocilia and the properties of MYO7A.

claim: MYO7A moves from pointed to barbed ends of actin filaments.
source: First, because MYO7A moves from pointed to barbed ends of actin filaments (Inoue and Ikebe, 2003), MYO7A may move PDZD7 and ADGRV1 towards stereocilia tips but stall if the N-terminal, extracellular end of ADGRV1 was anchored on the adjacent stereocilium.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Inoue and Ikebe, 2003.

claim: MYO7A may move PDZD7 and ADGRV1 towards stereocilia tips but stall if ADGRV1 is anchored on the adjacent stereocilium.
source: First, because MYO7A moves from pointed to barbed ends of actin filaments (Inoue and Ikebe, 2003), MYO7A may move PDZD7 and ADGRV1 towards stereocilia tips but stall if the N-terminal, extracellular end of ADGRV1 was anchored on the adjacent stereocilium.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: MYO7A could put ankle links under tension.
source: In this case, MYO7A would put ankle links under tension, which could also explain the frequent oblique positioning of the links (Goodyear and Richardson, 1992, 1999).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Goodyear and Richardson, 1992, 1999.

claim: MYO7A could hand off PDZD7 to MYO6 anywhere in the stereocilium.
source: Second, MYO7A could hand off PDZD7 to MYO6 anywhere in the stereocilium; because MYO6 moves towards pointed ends of actin filaments, it would properly localize the ankle-link proteins at stereocilia bases.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: MYO6 moves towards pointed ends of actin filaments.
source: Second, MYO7A could hand off PDZD7 to MYO6 anywhere in the stereocilium; because MYO6 moves towards pointed ends of actin filaments, it would properly localize the ankle-link proteins at stereocilia bases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MYO6 motor properties.

claim: MYO6 is thought to move PTPRQ to the taper region.
source: Indeed, MYO6 is thought to move PTPRQ to the taper region (Sakaguchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sakaguchi et al., 2008.

claim: MYO7A and MYO6 may be in a multimolecular, bidirectional motor complex.
source: Finally, MYO7A and MYO6 may be in a multimolecular, bidirectional motor complex; like with other bidirectional motor complexes (Hancock, 2014), reciprocal regulation of the two motors could steer the complex to the top or bottom of the stereocilia.
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Hancock, 2014.

claim: MYO6 was the most abundant protein co-precipitated with MYO7A.
source: Indeed, MYO6 was the most abundant protein co-precipitated with MYO7A, and we are presently investigating the specificity of this interaction.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The data show that MYO7A binds PDZD7 and is necessary for at least one step in its localization at the base of the hair bundle.
source: Regardless of the mechanism, the data here show that MYO7A binds PDZD7 and is necessary for at least one step in its localization at the base of the hair bundle.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the data in Figures 3-8.

claim: The paralogs PDZD7, USH1C, and DFNB31 are all deafness genes.
source: It is notable that the paralogs PDZD7, USH1C, and DFNB31 are all deafness genes and interact with MYO7A.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these genes.

claim: PDZD7 and DFNB31 both homodimerize and form heterodimers.
source: Moreover, PDZD7 and DFNB31 both homodimerize and form heterodimers (Chen et al., 2014); USH1C homodimerizes (Siemens et al., 2002), but whether it can heterodimerize with PDZD7 or DFNB31 is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014 and Siemens et al., 2002.

claim: USH1C homodimerizes.
source: Moreover, PDZD7 and DFNB31 both homodimerize and form heterodimers (Chen et al., 2014); USH1C homodimerizes (Siemens et al., 2002), but whether it can heterodimerize with PDZD7 or DFNB31 is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siemens et al., 2002.

claim: Whether USH1C can heterodimerize with PDZD7 or DFNB31 is unknown.
source: Moreover, PDZD7 and DFNB31 both homodimerize and form heterodimers (Chen et al., 2014); USH1C homodimerizes (Siemens et al., 2002), but whether it can heterodimerize with PDZD7 or DFNB31 is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: MYO7A contributes to the tip-link and ankle-link complexes.
source: Because other scaffolding proteins co-precipitate with MYO7A, these experiments show not only that MYO7A contributes to the tip-link and ankle-link complexes, but also suggest that MYO7A participates in other stereocilia protein complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry data.

claim: MYO7A participates in other stereocilia protein complexes beyond tip-link and ankle-link complexes.
source: Because other scaffolding proteins co-precipitate with MYO7A, these experiments show not only that MYO7A contributes to the tip-link and ankle-link complexes, but also suggest that MYO7A participates in other stereocilia protein complexes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mass spectrometry data showing multiple co-precipitating proteins.

claim: The coupled stereocilia-membrane purification and immunoaffinity isolation methods will be useful for isolating even very rare protein complexes from stereocilia.
source: Finally, the experiments indicate that the coupled stereocilia-membrane purification and immunoaffinity isolation methods will be useful for isolating even very rare protein complexes from stereocilia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the success of the methods described in the manuscript.
